---
title: "How do you know a model will work on data it has not seen?"
subtitle: "You will score models by hand first, then teach a computer to do it. All you need is arithmetic."
engine: knitr
---

You run a lemonade stand. Each dot below is one day: how many hours the sun shone, and how many jugs you sold. You want a model that, given tomorrow's sunshine, guesses tomorrow's sales.

The tree in the last lesson ended perfect on the data it learned from, and worse on fresh data. That is not bad luck. It happens to every model that is scored on the data it learned from. This lesson is about how to score a model honestly.

## Which of these two would you trust?

Two people fitted a curve to the same ten days. One drew a gentle curve. The other drew a wiggly one that passes through every dot.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="unseen-fits" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 1 · ten days at a lemonade stand, and two curves fitted to them · made-up data"}
:::

Press *measure the gentle one*, or click the gentle curve. A thread grows from each dot to the curve. Each thread is one miss: the jugs you really sold, minus the jugs the curve guessed.

To score a curve, square each miss and take the average. Squaring makes every miss count as positive, and makes big misses count more. Try two misses by hand, 1 and 3: 1 × 1 = 1, 3 × 3 = 9, and (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = **5**. Call this the **average squared miss**. Smaller is better.

Now press *measure the wiggly one*, or click the wiggly curve. It touches every dot, so every thread has length zero. Its score is 0.00, the best a score can be.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
Tomorrow brings a new day. Which curve would you trust to guess its sales?

- **The wiggly one.** Its score says it never misses. But it was fitted to these ten days, and then scored on the same ten days. That is like marking your own homework with the answers in front of you. Look at what it does between the dots.
- **The gentle one.** It misses every day by a little. But look at the wiggly one between the dots: it swoops up and down where there is no day to support it. A new day will land somewhere in those gaps.
:::

## What happens on points it has not seen?

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="unseen-fits" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 2 · the same two curves, scored on new days from the same stand · made-up data"}
:::

Press *bring 5 new days* a few times. The new days come from the same stand and the same weather, so they are drawn as crosses on the same picture. The threads now show the wiggly curve's misses on days it never saw.

Watch the "new" column. After ten new days the gentle curve's miss is about 0.7 and the wiggly one's is about 1.8. After all thirty it is 0.86 against 1.42. The curve with the perfect score loses.

The wiggly curve did not learn how sunshine sells lemonade. It learned these ten days, noise and all. The gentle curve learned less about these ten days, and more about the stand.

So here is the rule for this whole lesson: **a model's score on the data it learned from flatters it. To know how it will do next time, score it on days it never saw.**

## You do not have fresh points. Now what?

In Fig. 2 you could ask for new days whenever you liked. Real life is not so kind. You have the days you have: here, twenty of them.

So make some days new. Before the model sees anything, hide a few. Fit the model on the rest. Then score it on the ones you hid. To the model, the hidden days are as good as new.

Click cells in the strip to hide those days. You can click the dots too. Each time, the line is fitted again on the days you left showing, and scored on the ones you hid.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="cv-figure" data-step="0" data-caption="Fig. 3 · twenty days: hide some, fit a line on the rest, score it on the hidden ones · made-up data"}
:::

Look at the two scores beside the plot. Usually the miss on the hidden days is bigger than the miss on the days the line saw. The hidden score is the honest one.

### Now tell a computer

A computer needs the days as numbers. Each day is a pair, such as `(2.53, 2.89)`: 2.53 hours of sun and 2.89 jugs. `p[0]` is the first number of a pair and `p[1]` is the second.

The cell below fetches the twenty days, and the days you hid in Fig. 3. If you hid none, it uses five chosen for you. Python counts from 0, so the first cell in the strip is day 0.

Some Python words first. `def` gives a set of steps a name, so you can use them again. `for i in range(20)` repeats the indented lines with `i` set to 0, then 1, up to 19. `if` and `else` pick one of two paths. `[]` is an empty list, and `.append(x)` adds `x` to the end of it. `return` hands back the answer.

One blank is left. Replace it and press **Run**. The first time takes a few seconds while Python starts.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
from page import points, hidden          # the 20 days, and the days you hid in Fig. 3

def split(points, hidden):
    fit_on = []                          # days the model may learn from
    score_on = []                        # days kept out of its sight
    for i in range(len(points)):         # i counts the days: 0, 1, 2, ... 19
        if i in hidden:
            score_on.append(points[i])
        else:
            ____.append(points[i])       # every other day: which list does it go in?
    return fit_on, score_on

fit_on, score_on = split(points, hidden)
print("You hid days", hidden)
print("Fit on", len(fit_on), "days. Score on", len(score_on), "days.")

picture = {"points": fit_on + score_on,
           "labels": [0] * len(fit_on) + [2] * len(score_on),   # o to learn from, x hidden
           "xlim": (0, 10), "ylim": (0, 9), "xlabel": "hours of sun", "ylabel": "jugs sold"}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
from page import points, hidden          # the 20 days, and the days you hid in Fig. 3

def split(points, hidden):
    fit_on = []                          # days the model may learn from
    score_on = []                        # days kept out of its sight
    for i in range(len(points)):         # i counts the days: 0, 1, 2, ... 19
        if i in hidden:
            score_on.append(points[i])
        else:
            fit_on.append(points[i])     # every other day: the model may learn from it
    return fit_on, score_on

fit_on, score_on = split(points, hidden)
print("You hid days", hidden)
print("Fit on", len(fit_on), "days. Score on", len(score_on), "days.")

picture = {"points": fit_on + score_on,
           "labels": [0] * len(fit_on) + [2] * len(score_on),   # o to learn from, x hidden
           "xlim": (0, 10), "ylim": (0, 9), "xlabel": "hours of sun", "ylabel": "jugs sold"}
```
:::
:::

`len` counts what is in a list, and `[0] * 15` is a list of fifteen zeros: the picture uses those numbers to give each day its mark. The picture under the cell is drawn from the code's two lists: circles for the days the model may learn from, crosses for the hidden ones. It should match Fig. 3.

### Fit on the days it may see

Here are two models to compare. The **flat** model ignores the sun and always guesses the average sales. The **line** is the straight line you met in the lesson on fitting a line.

Both are stored the same way: a pair `(start, slope)`. The guess for a day with `x` hours of sun is start + slope × x. The flat model is just a line with slope 0.

The best line always passes through the middle of the days: the average sunshine and the average sales. Its slope comes from two sums, worked out in the code. Then the start has to put the line through the middle. Try it by hand. Say the middle is 5 hours and 4 jugs, and the slope is 0.5 jugs per hour. Going back from 5 hours to 0 hours loses 5 × 0.5 = 2.5 jugs, so the line starts at 4 − 2.5 = **1.5**.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def fit_flat(pts):
    total = 0
    for p in pts:
        total = total + p[1]              # add up the jugs sold
    return (total / len(pts), 0)          # start at the average, and never climb

def fit_line(pts):
    n = len(pts)
    total_x = 0
    total_y = 0
    for p in pts:
        total_x = total_x + p[0]
        total_y = total_y + p[1]
    mid_x = total_x / n                   # the average hours of sun
    mid_y = total_y / n                   # the average jugs sold
    together = 0                          # how sun and sales stray from the middle together
    spread = 0                            # how far the sun strays on its own
    for p in pts:
        dx = p[0] - mid_x
        dy = p[1] - mid_y
        together = together + dx * dy
        spread = spread + dx * dx
    slope = together / spread             # extra jugs for each extra hour of sun
    start = ____                          # the line must pass through (mid_x, mid_y)
    return (start, slope)

flat = fit_flat(fit_on)
line = fit_line(fit_on)
print("flat: always", round(flat[0], 2), "jugs")
print("line: starts at", round(line[0], 2), "and climbs", round(line[1], 2), "jugs per hour")

picture = {"points": fit_on,
           "lines": [[(0, flat[0]), (10, flat[0])]],
           "accent": [(0, line[0]), (10, line[0] + 10 * line[1])],
           "notes": ["level: the flat model", "sloped: the line"],
           "xlim": (0, 10), "ylim": (0, 9), "xlabel": "hours of sun", "ylabel": "jugs sold"}
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def fit_flat(pts):
    total = 0
    for p in pts:
        total = total + p[1]              # add up the jugs sold
    return (total / len(pts), 0)          # start at the average, and never climb

def fit_line(pts):
    n = len(pts)
    total_x = 0
    total_y = 0
    for p in pts:
        total_x = total_x + p[0]
        total_y = total_y + p[1]
    mid_x = total_x / n                   # the average hours of sun
    mid_y = total_y / n                   # the average jugs sold
    together = 0                          # how sun and sales stray from the middle together
    spread = 0                            # how far the sun strays on its own
    for p in pts:
        dx = p[0] - mid_x
        dy = p[1] - mid_y
        together = together + dx * dy
        spread = spread + dx * dx
    slope = together / spread             # extra jugs for each extra hour of sun
    start = mid_y - slope * mid_x         # the line must pass through (mid_x, mid_y)
    return (start, slope)

flat = fit_flat(fit_on)
line = fit_line(fit_on)
print("flat: always", round(flat[0], 2), "jugs")
print("line: starts at", round(line[0], 2), "and climbs", round(line[1], 2), "jugs per hour")

picture = {"points": fit_on,
           "lines": [[(0, flat[0]), (10, flat[0])]],
           "accent": [(0, line[0]), (10, line[0] + 10 * line[1])],
           "notes": ["level: the flat model", "sloped: the line"],
           "xlim": (0, 10), "ylim": (0, 9), "xlabel": "hours of sun", "ylabel": "jugs sold"}
```
:::
:::

Notice that both models were fitted on `fit_on` only. Neither has seen a hidden day.

### How far off is it on the hidden days?

Scoring means the average squared miss from the start of the lesson.

::: {.ask}
Before you write code for it: how would you check that the code scores correctly?

- **Run it on the twenty days.** You would get a number, and no way of telling whether it is right.
- **Try a case I can do by hand.** Yes. Take the line that starts at 2 and climbs 1 per hour. A day with 1 hour of sun and 4 jugs: the line guesses 2 + 1 = 3, a miss of 1. A day with 3 hours and 8 jugs: it guesses 5, a miss of 3. Squared and averaged, that is (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5. If the code says anything else, it is wrong.
:::

The first line the cell prints is that hand example. The function at the end, `drawing`, only builds the picture under the cell; you can skim it. (`str` turns a number into text, so it can be written beside the plot.)

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def predict(model, x):
    return model[0] + model[1] * x        # start, plus slope times the hours of sun

def miss(model, pts):
    total = 0
    for p in pts:
        off = p[1] - ____                 # the jugs really sold, minus the model's guess
        total = total + off * off         # square it and add it up
    return total / len(pts)               # the average squared miss

print(miss((2, 1), [(1, 4), (3, 8)]))     # by hand this was 5

print("line, on the days it saw: ", round(miss(line, fit_on), 2))
print("line, on the hidden days: ", round(miss(line, score_on), 2))
print("flat, on the hidden days: ", round(miss(flat, score_on), 2))

def drawing(seen, unseen, model, notes):
    threads = []
    for p in unseen:
        threads.append((p, (p[0], predict(model, p[0]))))     # from the day to the line
    return {"points": seen + unseen,
            "labels": [0] * len(seen) + [2] * len(unseen),
            "accent": [(0, predict(model, 0)), (10, predict(model, 10))],
            "segments": threads, "notes": notes,
            "xlim": (0, 10), "ylim": (0, 9), "xlabel": "hours of sun", "ylabel": "jugs sold"}

picture = drawing(fit_on, score_on, line, ["hidden: " + str(round(miss(line, score_on), 2))])
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def predict(model, x):
    return model[0] + model[1] * x        # start, plus slope times the hours of sun

def miss(model, pts):
    total = 0
    for p in pts:
        off = p[1] - predict(model, p[0]) # the jugs really sold, minus the model's guess
        total = total + off * off         # square it and add it up
    return total / len(pts)               # the average squared miss

print(miss((2, 1), [(1, 4), (3, 8)]))     # by hand this was 5

print("line, on the days it saw: ", round(miss(line, fit_on), 2))
print("line, on the hidden days: ", round(miss(line, score_on), 2))
print("flat, on the hidden days: ", round(miss(flat, score_on), 2))

def drawing(seen, unseen, model, notes):
    threads = []
    for p in unseen:
        threads.append((p, (p[0], predict(model, p[0]))))     # from the day to the line
    return {"points": seen + unseen,
            "labels": [0] * len(seen) + [2] * len(unseen),
            "accent": [(0, predict(model, 0)), (10, predict(model, 10))],
            "segments": threads, "notes": notes,
            "xlim": (0, 10), "ylim": (0, 9), "xlabel": "hours of sun", "ylabel": "jugs sold"}

picture = drawing(fit_on, score_on, line, ["hidden: " + str(round(miss(line, score_on), 2))])
```
:::
:::

Compare the two line scores it prints with the two scores beside Fig. 3. Same days, same hidden ones, same sums: they should agree. And the flat model does worse on the hidden days than the line, which is what you would hope from a model that ignores the sun.

## Would a different split give the same score?

You chose which days to hide. Someone else would have hidden different ones. Does that change the score?

Here is the same line, scored on eight different splits. Each time, `random.sample(range(20), 5)` picks five of the twenty days at random to hide. `random.seed(4)` makes the "random" picks the same every time you run it, and `min` and `max` find the smallest and largest score.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot" data-aside="true"}
```python
import random
random.seed(4)                            # the same "random" picks on every run

scores = []
bars = []
for attempt in range(8):
    held = random.sample(range(20), 5)    # five days, picked at random, to hide
    fit_part, score_part = split(points, held)
    model = fit_line(fit_part)            # fit on the other 15
    score = round(miss(model, score_part), 2)
    scores.append(score)
    bars.append((attempt + 1, score))     # one bar for each split

print(scores)
print("lowest", min(scores), "and highest", max(scores))

picture = {"bars": bars,
           "xlabel": "split", "ylabel": "miss on the hidden days",
           "notes": ["lowest " + str(min(scores)), "highest " + str(max(scores))]}
```
:::

Same days. Same line. Same recipe. The scores run from 0.16 to 1.15: the highest is seven times the lowest. In Fig. 3 you saw the same thing: hide different days and the hidden score jumps.

So one split is partly luck. Hide a few easy days and the model looks great. Hide a few odd ones and it looks poor.

::: {.ask}
Eight splits, eight scores. Which one is the line's real score?

- **The lowest one.** Tempting, and wrong for the reason the whole lesson is about: picking the best-looking number flatters the model.
- **The first one.** That is what you get with a single split. It is no more right than the other seven. It just came first.
- **None of them on its own.** Yes. Each score is the true score plus some luck from which days were hidden. Use many scores and the luck starts to cancel out. And make sure every day gets hidden once, so no day is left out of the scoring.
:::

## How do you use every day for scoring?

Take turns. Cut the twenty days into parts, say five parts of four days. Hide part 1, fit on the other four parts, score on part 1. Then hide part 2 and do the same. Carry on until every part has been hidden once. The final score is the average of the five.

Every day is hidden exactly once. Every day is learned from four times.

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="cv-figure" data-step="1" data-caption="Fig. 4 · taking turns: each part of the strip is hidden once · made-up data"}
:::

Press *next part*, or drag the hatching along the strip, and watch it move. The line moves too, because each turn it is fitted on different days. The small chart in the column collects each part's miss, and the tall tick marks their average. Press *run all* to finish the round.

The parts disagree with each other, just like the random splits did. But now you are not trusting any one of them. You are averaging all of them, and every day took part.

In code, `take_turns` is the same loop. It is handed a fitting function, `fit_line` or `fit_flat`, and uses whichever it is given; a function can be passed around like any other value. `20 // 5` is whole-number division: 4.

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
def take_turns(points, k, fit):
    size = len(points) // k               # days in each part: 20 // 5 is 4
    scores = []
    pictures = []
    for part in range(k):                 # part 0, then 1, ... up to k - 1
        first = part * size               # where this part starts in the strip
        held = range(first, first + size) # the days in this part
        fit_part, score_part = split(points, held)
        model = fit(fit_part)             # learn from the other parts
        scores.append(miss(model, score_part))
        note = "part " + str(part + 1) + ": " + str(round(scores[part], 2))
        pictures.append(drawing(fit_part, score_part, model, [note]))
    return scores, pictures

scores, frames = take_turns(points, 5, fit_line)
for part in range(5):
    print("part", part + 1, "hidden, miss", round(scores[part], 2))
print("average of the 5:", round(sum(scores) / ____, 2))
```
::: {.py-solution}
```python
def take_turns(points, k, fit):
    size = len(points) // k               # days in each part: 20 // 5 is 4
    scores = []
    pictures = []
    for part in range(k):                 # part 0, then 1, ... up to k - 1
        first = part * size               # where this part starts in the strip
        held = range(first, first + size) # the days in this part
        fit_part, score_part = split(points, held)
        model = fit(fit_part)             # learn from the other parts
        scores.append(miss(model, score_part))
        note = "part " + str(part + 1) + ": " + str(round(scores[part], 2))
        pictures.append(drawing(fit_part, score_part, model, [note]))
    return scores, pictures

scores, frames = take_turns(points, 5, fit_line)
for part in range(5):
    print("part", part + 1, "hidden, miss", round(scores[part], 2))
print("average of the 5:", round(sum(scores) / len(scores), 2))
```
:::
:::

The picture plays back each turn: the crosses move from part to part, and the line is refitted each time. Compare the five scores and their average with Fig. 4 after *run all*. They should be the same numbers.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The same thing in symbols"}
With $y_i$ for the jugs really sold on day $i$, $\hat y_i$ for the model's guess, and $n$ days, the average squared miss is

$$\text{miss} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat y_i)^2$$

With $k$ parts and $\text{miss}_j$ for the score when part $j$ is hidden, the score from taking turns is

$$\text{score}(k) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \text{miss}_j$$

Read the big Σ as "add these up", and the hat on $\hat y$ as "the model's guess for".
:::

### How many parts?

Slide *parts* in Fig. 4. With 2 parts, each line learns from only half the days, so it is a weaker line than the one you will finally use. With 20 parts, one day each, every line learns from 19 days, but you have to fit twenty lines, and each score rests on a single day, so the scores jump about.

Five or ten parts is the usual choice. It almost always works well enough. On a small data set use fewer, so that each part still has a few days in it.

## What if you use the hidden data to choose between models?

So far you scored one model. Usually you are choosing: the flat model or the line? A line or a curve? How many neighbours, how wide a gap, how deep a tree? You take turns with each candidate, and keep the one with the lowest score.

::: {.ask data-veil="true"}
Five candidates take turns. The lowest score wins. Is the winner's score a fair guess of how it will do next time?

- **Yes, it was scored on hidden days.** It was. But you looked at five scores and picked the smallest. Each score is part skill and part luck, and the smallest is likely to be the one with the best luck. Now it is the winner's score that flatters it.
- **No, it is still too kind.** Right. Picking the lowest of several scores picks good luck along with skill. To find out how the winner really does, you need days that played no part in picking it.
:::

::: {.ink-figure data-figure="cv-figure" data-step="2" data-caption="Fig. 5 · fit and choose inside the first fifteen days; the last five stay locked until the end · made-up data"}
:::

The last five cells are locked before anything else happens. Inside the first fifteen, five candidates take turns, three parts of five days each: the flat model, the line, and curves that can bend more and more. "Curve 2" can bend once, like the gentle curve in Fig. 1. The lowest score wins.

Then the winner is fitted once more, on all fifteen days, and *open the final part* (or a click on the locked cells) scores it on the five locked days. That is the only time those days are used.

Beside it, the same recipe runs on 300 more made-up stands. On average the winner's score from taking turns is 0.78, and its final check is 0.96. The score you chose by looks better than the model really is. The final check is the honest number.

So there are three jobs, and each one needs days the earlier jobs did not use:

1. **Fit.** Each candidate learns from some days.
2. **Choose.** Each candidate is scored on days it did not learn from, by taking turns. The lowest score wins.
3. **Final check.** The winner is scored once on days that were locked away from the start.

The taking turns happens *inside* the first fifteen days. The final five are never part of a turn. They are not a third kind of part. They sit outside the whole fit-and-choose process, and they are opened once, at the very end. If you look at them earlier and change your choice, they have become part of the choosing, and you have no honest number left.

Here is the whole recipe in code. `points[:15]` means the first fifteen days, and `points[15:]` means from day 15 to the end. One blank: which days does the final check use?

::: {.py-cell data-draw="py-plot"}
```python
fitting_days = points[:15]                # fit and choose happen in here
final_days = points[15:]                  # locked away until the very end

flat_scores, flat_pictures = take_turns(fitting_days, 3, fit_flat)
line_scores, line_pictures = take_turns(fitting_days, 3, fit_line)
flat_score = sum(flat_scores) / 3
line_score = sum(line_scores) / 3
print("taking turns, flat:", round(flat_score, 2))
print("taking turns, line:", round(line_score, 2))

if line_score < flat_score:               # choose: the lower score wins
    winner = fit_line(fitting_days)       # fit the winner again, on all 15 days
    won_with = line_score
else:
    winner = fit_flat(fitting_days)
    won_with = flat_score

final_score = miss(winner, ____)          # the one and only look at the locked days
print("the winner's score when chosen:", round(won_with, 2))
print("its final check:", round(final_score, 2))

frames = line_pictures + [drawing(fitting_days, final_days, winner, ["final check: " + str(round(final_score, 2))])]
```
::: {.py-solution}

The flat and line scores it prints are the first two rows beside Fig. 5. Your code tried only two candidates, so the line wins, where the figure, with five, picked curve 2. The pattern is the same in both: the final check is worse than the score the winner was chosen by. The picture plays the line's three turns, then the final check, with the locked days as crosses.

## What you just built

Everything you did has a name:

| What you did | What it is called |
|:--|:--|
| The average squared miss | Mean squared error (MSE) |
| Perfect on the days it learned from, worse on new days | Overfitting |
| The days a model learns from | The training set |
| Hiding some days, fitting on the rest, scoring on the hidden ones | A train/test split, or holdout |
| The parts of the strip | Folds |
| Taking turns, then averaging the scores | *k*-fold cross-validation |
| One day per part | Leave-one-out cross-validation |
| Scoring candidates to pick one | Validation, or model selection (tuning) |
| The final part, locked away until the end | The test set |
| The winner's score flattering it | Optimistic bias |
| Curve 2, curve 3, curve 4 | Polynomials of degree 2, 3 and 4 |

The training data, where cross-validation happens, and the test set, held out, are the only two piles. Cross-validation is something you do inside the training data, not a third pile. A common split keeps 70 to 80 percent of the rows for training and 20 to 30 percent for the test set. When the model sorts things into classes instead of guessing a number, the miss on each part is usually the fraction it got wrong.

A library such as scikit-learn has all of this ready: `train_test_split` hides the rows, `KFold` cuts the parts, and `cross_val_score` takes the turns and hands back the scores. It can shuffle the rows before cutting the parts (your twenty days were already in no particular order), and it works with any kind of model. You could now read what it does and recognise every step.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reference: the same ideas in R"}
Every plot below is produced by the R on this page. Open "The R" under any of them to see the code.

Twenty noisy points from a simple curve, with a degree-15 polynomial and a degree-3 polynomial fitted to all of them.

```{r}
#| label: plot-overfitting-demo
#| fig-cap: "The wiggly model fits training data perfectly but is clearly wrong"

library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

# True relationship: simple curve
x <- sort(runif(20, 0, 10))
y <- 2 * sin(x) + rnorm(20, 0, 0.8)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Overfit model: high-degree polynomial
fit_over <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 15), data = df)
# Good model: low-degree polynomial
fit_good <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = df)

x_grid <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
pred_over <- predict(fit_over, newdata = data.frame(x = x_grid))
pred_good <- predict(fit_good, newdata = data.frame(x = x_grid))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = x_grid, y = pred_over),
            aes(x, y), color = "coral", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = x_grid, y = pred_good),
            aes(x, y), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = x_grid, y = 2 * sin(x_grid)),
            aes(x, y), color = "gray50", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 8.5, y = 4, label = "Overfit (degree 15)",
           color = "coral", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.5, y = -1, label = "Good fit (degree 3)",
           color = "steelblue", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = -2.5, label = "True function",
           color = "gray50", size = 3.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", title = "Training accuracy is misleading")
```

A random 70/30 split of forty points into training and test.

```{r}
#| label: plot-train-test-split
#| fig-cap: "Split data into training (build the model) and test (evaluate it)"

set.seed(7)
n <- 40
x_all <- sort(runif(n, 0, 10))
y_all <- 2 * sin(x_all) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)

# Random 70/30 split
train_idx <- sample(n, round(0.7 * n))
test_idx <- setdiff(1:n, train_idx)

df_all <- data.frame(
  x = x_all, y = y_all,
  set = ifelse(1:n %in% train_idx, "Train", "Test")
)

ggplot(df_all, aes(x, y, color = set, shape = set)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("coral", "steelblue")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 19)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y",
    title = paste0("70/30 split: ", length(train_idx), " train, ",
                   length(test_idx), " test"))
```

Both models fitted on the training points only, then scored on both sets. The overfit model is the one whose two bars disagree.

```{r}
#| label: plot-train-test-eval
#| fig-cap: "Overfit model: great on train, terrible on test. Good model: consistent on both."

df_train <- df_all[df_all$set == "Train", ]
df_test <- df_all[df_all$set == "Test", ]

# Overfit
fit_over <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 15), data = df_train)
# Good
fit_good <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = df_train)

# Errors
results <- data.frame(
  Model = rep(c("Overfit (degree 15)", "Good (degree 3)"), each = 2),
  Set = rep(c("Train", "Test"), 2),
  RMSE = c(
    sqrt(mean(residuals(fit_over)^2)),
    sqrt(mean((df_test$y - predict(fit_over, df_test))^2)),
    sqrt(mean(residuals(fit_good)^2)),
    sqrt(mean((df_test$y - predict(fit_good, df_test))^2))
  )
)

ggplot(results, aes(x = Model, y = RMSE, fill = Set)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("coral", "steelblue")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(y = "RMSE (lower = better)", title = "The reveal: test performance exposes overfitting") +
  coord_flip()
```

The same degree-3 model scored on twenty different random splits. The score moves with the split.

```{r}
#| label: plot-split-variance
#| fig-cap: "Different random splits give different test scores — which one is 'right'?"

set.seed(1)
scores <- sapply(1:20, function(i) {
  idx <- sample(n, round(0.7 * n))
  train <- data.frame(x = x_all[idx], y = y_all[idx])
  test <- data.frame(x = x_all[-idx], y = y_all[-idx])
  fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = train)
  sqrt(mean((test$y - predict(fit, test))^2))
})

ggplot(data.frame(trial = 1:20, rmse = scores), aes(trial, rmse)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(scores), color = "coral", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 17, y = mean(scores) + 0.1,
           label = paste0("Average: ", round(mean(scores), 2)),
           color = "coral", size = 4) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Random Split #", y = "Test RMSE",
       title = "Same model, 20 different splits → 20 different scores")
```

Five rounds of 5-fold cross-validation as a grid. The block marked TEST in each row is the held-out fold of that round, not the test set.

```{r}
#| label: plot-kfold-diagram
#| fig-cap: "5-fold cross-validation: each fold takes a turn as the test set"

# Visual diagram of k-fold CV
k <- 5
fold_colors <- c("coral", "steelblue")

par(mar = c(2, 6, 3, 2))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, k), ylim = c(0.5, k + 0.5),
     xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     main = "5-Fold Cross-Validation")

for (round in 1:k) {
  for (fold in 1:k) {
    col <- ifelse(fold == round,
      adjustcolor("coral", 0.8),
      adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.4))
    rect(fold - 1, k - round + 0.6, fold, k - round + 1.4, col = col, border = "white", lwd = 2)
    label <- ifelse(fold == round, "TEST", "train")
    text(fold - 0.5, k - round + 1, label, cex = 0.9,
         col = ifelse(fold == round, "white", "white"),
         font = ifelse(fold == round, 2, 1))
  }
  text(-0.3, k - round + 1, paste("Round", round), cex = 0.8, adj = 1)
}

text(k / 2, 0.3, "→ Average all 5 scores = cross-validation estimate", cex = 1, font = 2)
```

The cross-validation score for 3, 5, 10, 25 and $n$ folds, each repeated thirty times with different fold assignments to show how much the estimate moves.

```{r}
#| label: plot-fold-comparison
#| fig-cap: "More folds = more stable estimate, but diminishing returns past 10"

set.seed(42)
n <- 50
x <- sort(runif(n, 0, 10))
y <- 2 * sin(x) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)
df_cv <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Run k-fold CV for different k values, repeat to see variance
fold_vals <- c(3, 5, 10, 25, n)
fold_labels <- c("3", "5", "10", "25", paste0(n, "\n(LOO)"))

results_list <- list()
for (fi in seq_along(fold_vals)) {
  kf <- fold_vals[fi]
  scores <- sapply(1:30, function(rep) {
    folds <- sample(rep(1:kf, length.out = n))
    errs <- sapply(1:kf, function(f) {
      train <- df_cv[folds != f, ]
      test <- df_cv[folds == f, ]
      if (nrow(train) < 4 || nrow(test) < 1) return(NA)
      fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3), data = train)
      mean((test$y - predict(fit, test))^2)
    })
    mean(errs, na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  results_list[[fi]] <- data.frame(
    folds = fold_labels[fi],
    score = scores
  )
}

results_all <- do.call(rbind, results_list)
results_all$folds <- factor(results_all$folds, levels = fold_labels)

ggplot(results_all, aes(folds, score)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, outlier.size = 1) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Number of Folds", y = "CV Score (MSE)",
       title = "More folds = less variance in the estimate")
```

Cross-validation used to choose a parameter: 5-fold accuracy for ten values of $k$ in KNN.

```{r}
#| label: plot-tune-k-knn
#| fig-cap: "Cross-validation finds the best k for KNN by testing each value"

library(class)
set.seed(42)

# Generate classification data
df_class <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(rnorm(50, 2, 1), rnorm(50, 4.5, 1)),
  x2 = c(rnorm(50, 2, 1), rnorm(50, 4.5, 1)),
  group = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 50))
)

# 5-fold CV for different k values
k_values <- c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21, 31, 45)
n_obs <- nrow(df_class)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_obs))

cv_results <- sapply(k_values, function(k_nn) {
  fold_acc <- sapply(1:5, function(f) {
    train <- df_class[folds != f, ]
    test <- df_class[folds == f, ]
    pred <- knn(train[, 1:2], test[, 1:2], train$group, k = k_nn)
    mean(pred == test$group)
  })
  mean(fold_acc)
})

best_k <- k_values[which.max(cv_results)]

ggplot(data.frame(k = k_values, accuracy = cv_results), aes(k, accuracy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_k, linetype = "dashed", color = "coral") +
  annotate("text", x = best_k + 3, y = min(cv_results) + 0.01,
           label = paste0("Best k = ", best_k), color = "coral", size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_values) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "k (number of neighbors)", y = "CV Accuracy (5-fold)",
       title = "Using cross-validation to choose k in KNN")
```

The same folds used to choose C for a linear SVM.

```{r}
#| label: plot-tune-c-svm
#| fig-cap: "Same idea for SVM: cross-validate over different C values"

library(e1071)

c_values <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000)

cv_svm <- sapply(c_values, function(C) {
  fold_acc <- sapply(1:5, function(f) {
    train <- df_class[folds != f, ]
    test <- df_class[folds == f, ]
    fit <- svm(group ~ x1 + x2, data = train, kernel = "linear", cost = C)
    pred <- predict(fit, test)
    mean(pred == test$group)
  })
  mean(fold_acc)
})

best_c <- c_values[which.max(cv_svm)]

ggplot(data.frame(C = c_values, accuracy = cv_svm), aes(C, accuracy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_c, linetype = "dashed", color = "coral") +
  annotate("text", x = best_c * 5, y = min(cv_svm) + 0.005,
           label = paste0("Best C = ", best_c), color = "coral", size = 4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "C (cost parameter, log scale)", y = "CV Accuracy (5-fold)",
       title = "Using cross-validation to choose C in SVM")
```

The whole workflow in one chunk: hold out a test set, cross-validate on the rest to choose $k$, then score once on the test set.

```{r}
#| label: plot-full-workflow
#| fig-cap: "The complete model-building workflow with cross-validation"

# Simulate the full workflow
set.seed(42)

# Step 1: Hold out test set
test_idx <- sample(n_obs, round(0.2 * n_obs))
train_val <- df_class[-test_idx, ]
test_final <- df_class[test_idx, ]

# Step 2: CV on train_val to find best k
folds_tv <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(train_val)))

cv_k <- sapply(k_values, function(k_nn) {
  fold_acc <- sapply(1:5, function(f) {
    tr <- train_val[folds_tv != f, ]
    va <- train_val[folds_tv == f, ]
    pred <- knn(tr[, 1:2], va[, 1:2], tr$group, k = k_nn)
    mean(pred == va$group)
  })
  mean(fold_acc)
})

best_k_final <- k_values[which.max(cv_k)]

# Step 3: Evaluate on test set with best k
test_pred <- knn(train_val[, 1:2], test_final[, 1:2], train_val$group, k = best_k_final)
test_acc <- mean(test_pred == test_final$group)

cat(sprintf("Best k from CV: %d\n", best_k_final))
cat(sprintf("CV accuracy (validation): %.1f%%\n", max(cv_k) * 100))
cat(sprintf("Final test accuracy: %.1f%%\n", test_acc * 100))
cat("\nIf these two numbers are close → model generalizes well")
cat("\nIf test << CV → you overfit during tuning (rare with proper CV)")
```

Training $R^2$ against cross-validated $R^2$ as the polynomial degree grows. Training only goes up; validation turns over.

```{r}
#| label: plot-overfit-gap
#| fig-cap: "The gap between training and validation accuracy reveals overfitting"

# Show train vs validation accuracy across model complexity
complexities <- 1:15
train_acc <- numeric(15)
val_acc <- numeric(15)

set.seed(42)
folds_gap <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(df_cv)))

for (d in complexities) {
  # Training accuracy (full data)
  fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d), data = df_cv)
  train_acc[d] <- 1 - mean(residuals(fit)^2) / var(df_cv$y)

  # CV accuracy
  fold_r2 <- sapply(1:5, function(f) {
    tr <- df_cv[folds_gap != f, ]
    te <- df_cv[folds_gap == f, ]
    if (nrow(tr) < d + 1) return(NA)
    fit_cv <- lm(y ~ poly(x, min(d, nrow(tr) - 2)), data = tr)
    pred <- predict(fit_cv, te)
    1 - mean((te$y - pred)^2) / var(te$y)
  })
  val_acc[d] <- mean(fold_r2, na.rm = TRUE)
}

gap_df <- data.frame(
  complexity = rep(complexities, 2),
  r_squared = c(train_acc, val_acc),
  set = rep(c("Training", "Validation (CV)"), each = 15)
)

ggplot(gap_df, aes(complexity, r_squared, color = set)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = which.max(val_acc), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  annotate("text", x = which.max(val_acc) + 1.5, y = 0.3,
           label = paste0("Best complexity = ", which.max(val_acc)),
           color = "gray40", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 0.85, label = "OVERFIT ZONE",
           color = "coral", size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  labs(x = "Model Complexity (polynomial degree)", y = "R²",
       color = "Evaluated on", title = "Training R² always goes up — validation reveals the truth")
```

Leave-one-out on six points: each panel fits the line without one point and measures the miss on that point.

```{r}
#| label: plot-loocv
#| fig-cap: "LOOCV: each point gets a turn as the sole test point"

# Visual: highlight one point at a time
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1))

set.seed(42)
small_df <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8),
  y = c(2.1, 3.8, 4.5, 7.2, 8.1, 10.5)
)

for (i in 1:6) {
  train <- small_df[-i, ]
  test <- small_df[i, ]
  fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = train)

  plot(small_df$x, small_df$y, pch = 19, cex = 1.5,
    col = ifelse(1:6 == i, "coral", "steelblue"),
    main = paste("Round", i, "— test point", i),
    xlab = "x", ylab = "y", xlim = c(0, 9), ylim = c(0, 12))
  abline(fit, col = "gray50")
  pred <- predict(fit, test)
  segments(test$x, test$y, test$x, pred, col = "coral", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  text(test$x + 0.5, (test$y + pred) / 2,
       paste0("err=", round(abs(test$y - pred), 2)),
       col = "coral", cex = 0.8)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
